title: The stall is not a problem
summary: When a brisket or pork shoulder gets stuck around 160°F for hours, don't panic. The meat is just sweating. Wrap it if you're in a hurry, or wait it out for better bark.

body.text: Every long cook hits a wall somewhere between 150 and 170 degrees. The meat sweats, and that sweat cools it down, same as you on a hot day. It's normal, and it passes.

body.heading: Wrap when you need to, not because you're scared
body.text: Butcher paper lets some steam out so the bark stays firm. Foil works faster but softens the bark. You don't have to wrap at all. If the bark looks dark and dinner can wait, just let it ride.

body.heading: What the stall isn't
body.text: It isn't the fat melting. The tough, chewy stuff inside the meat doesn't even start breaking down until closer to 180 or 200. The stall is just moisture sitting on the surface.

takeaways: A big brisket or pork butt can stall for 2 to 4 hours.
Only wrap after the bark is dark and set, and only if you're short on time.
Paper keeps the bark firm. Foil softens it. Pick the one you want.

title: Bark is a crust you earn
summary: Bark is the dark, tasty crust on smoked meat: dried rub, melted fat, and smoke. If it wipes off when you touch it, it wasn't done yet.

body.text: Good bark looks like dark leather. Wait until the rub feels dry and stuck on before you wrap. Wrap too early and you'll unwrap soggy seasoning instead of bark.

takeaways: Don't wrap until the bark is dark and set. Ever.

title: Thin blue smoke or go home
summary: Thick white smoke means your wood isn't burning clean. Feed the fire small pieces of wood, often, and keep a flame going.

body.text: Bad smoke comes from a bad fire, not bad wood. Use small splits, add them often, and always keep a flame you can see.

takeaways: If folks down the street can see your smoke, it's too thick.

title: Temperature is a rumor
summary: 203°F is a guess, not a rule. The meat is done when a probe slides in easy.

body.text: Stick a probe or thermometer into the flat part of the brisket. If you have to push, it ain't done. If it slides in like warm butter, pull it off.

title: Resting is still cooking
summary: Cut a brisket the minute it's done and all the juice runs out. Let it rest and it stays juicy.

body.text: Leave it whole, don't slice yet. Put it in a dry cooler or a 150°F oven for at least an hour. Two to four hours is even better.

takeaways: Rest it longer than you think you need to.

title: Match the wood to the animal
summary: Post oak for beef, hickory for pork, fruitwood for chicken and turkey. Go easy on mesquite. A little goes a long way.

body.text: A chunk of mesquite on a quick steak cook tastes great. But twelve hours of mesquite will overpower everything on the pit.

takeaways: Use dry, seasoned wood. Never green wood.

title: Fat cap up, down, or does it matter?
summary: Put the fat cap toward the heat so it shields the meat. But fat doesn't drip down through the meat and baste it, no matter what folks say.

body.text: On an offset smoker, point the thick end toward the firebox. The fat protects the meat from the heat. That's all it does.

takeaways: Trim the fat to about a quarter of an inch. But be sure not to remove all the fat.

title: Spritz, mop, or leave it alone
summary: Most folks spray their meat way too much.

body.text: Once the bark is set, a light mist every 45 to 60 minutes is plenty. And leave it completely alone for the first 3 to 4 hours.

takeaways: Don't spray so much you wash the crust off.

title: Salt early, sugar late
summary: Salting the meat the night before is the easiest way to make it taste better, and it costs nothing.

body.text: Salt it the night before if you can. Save anything sugary for a glaze near the end. Sugar burns over a long cook.

takeaways: Salt the night before. Free flavor.

title: What the circuit doesn't tell you
summary: Competition barbecue is one fancy bite for judges. Backyard barbecue is dinner for people you love.

body.text: Take the good ideas from the competition cooks and leave the rest. Burn your wood clean so the smoke stays thin, not thick and white. Rest the meat for real. And be patient with the bark, let it turn dark before you wrap. Skip the injections and the fancy tricks unless you enjoy doing them.

takeaways: You're feeding a table, not chasing a scorecard.
